sections.label: Bills debate and court survey
sections.summary: Members may raise questions on three Bills during debate, and formal Second Readings will follow; a 2015 survey found 92% trust in the legal system.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: Members will be welcome to raise questions or express their views on the three Bills during the debate.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: And we will still have the formal Second Readings of the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore (Amendment) Bill and also the Judges' Remuneration (Amendment) Bill to ensure that the procedural requirements are dealt with.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: In a survey conducted by my Ministry in late 2015 on how Singaporeans view the Courts, 92% said they trust and had confidence in our legal system.

sections.label: Court of Appeal filings 2018
sections.summary: In 2018, the number of matters filed to the Court of Appeal increased to 490.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: In 2018, the number of matters filed to the Court of Appeal increased to 490.

sections.label: Establishing Appellate Division of High Court
sections.summary: The Bill, with the Constitution (Amendment) Bill and Judges' Remuneration (Amendment) Bill, will establish an Appellate Division of the High Court.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: However, we feel that these are just stop gap measures and a more long-lasting sustainable change would be useful.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: This Bill, together with the Constitution (Amendment) Bill and the Judges' Remuneration (Amendment) Bill, will establish an Appellate Division of the High Court.

sections.label: General Division jurisdiction and powers
sections.summary: The General Division will have all the jurisdiction and powers of the existing High Court and hear all its original and appellate cases.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The General Division will have all the jurisdiction and powers of the existing High Court and will hear all cases that fall within the original and appellate jurisdiction of the existing High Court.

sections.label: Prescribed civil appeals Sixth Schedule
sections.summary: Prescribed categories of civil appeals are set out in legislation and will be in a new Sixth Schedule to the amended SCJA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: So, under written law, that is set out in legislation and in prescribed categories of civil appeals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: These prescribed categories will be set out in a new Sixth Schedule to the amended Supreme Court of Judicature Act (SCJA).

sections.label: Categories of prescribed appeals
sections.summary: The prescribed appeals generally concern substantial consequences, public interest questions of law, administration of justice, novel questions, important issues, or strategic areas.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The appeals that have been prescribed are generally those that: (a)	are likely to have substantial consequences for individuals or society; (b) may involve questions of law of public interest which would benefit from guidance of the apex Court in Singapore; (c)	concern the general administration of justice; (d)	may involve novel questions of law, or new areas of law which would benefit from guidance from the Court of Appeal; (e)	may involve issues that are likely to be important and require earlier clarification from the Court of Appeal; or (f)	relate to strategic areas that would benefit from the stature of the apex Court, such as the areas of laws which seek to bolster Singapore's status as a dispute resolution hub or debt restructuring hub.

sections.label: Further appeals need Court of Appeal leave
sections.summary: A further appeal against an Appellate Division decision may only be brought with the leave of the Court of Appeal.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Where an appeal has been heard and decided by the Appellate Division, any further appeal against the decision of the Appellate Division may only be brought with the leave of the Court of Appeal.

sections.label: Leave requires point of public importance
sections.summary: The Court of Appeal will consider granting leave only if the appeal raises a point of law of public importance.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The Court of Appeal will consider granting leave only if the appeal raises a point of law of public importance.

sections.label: Paper hearings with parties' consent
sections.summary: The Appellate Division and Court of Appeal may decide specified categories of appeals without oral arguments if all parties consent.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The Bills expand the categories of cases that can be decided on paper in three ways.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: First, the Appellate Division and the Court of Appeal will have the powers to decide specified categories of appeals without hearing oral arguments, if all parties to the appeal consent.

sections.label: Two-Judge coram paper hearing
sections.summary: The Appellate Division may decide any appeal without oral arguments if all parties consent to a two-Judge coram and paper hearing.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Second, the Appellate Division will be able to decide any appeal without hearing oral arguments if all parties to the appeal consent to a two-Judge coram and to a paper hearing.

sections.label: Five interlocutory orders made appealable
sections.summary: The Bill makes five interlocutory orders at paragraphs 1(c) to (g) of the Fourth Schedule appealable with leave of the Appellate Court.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Fourth, the Bill makes five interlocutory orders at paragraphs 1(c) to (g) of the existing Fourth Schedule of the SCJA appealable with the leave of the Appellate Court.

sections.label: Court of Appeal transfer to Appellate Division
sections.summary: New section 29E(1) allows the Court of Appeal to transfer to the Appellate Division any civil appeal made to it.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: First, the new section 29E(1) proposed by the SCJA Bill allows the Court of Appeal to transfer to the Appellate Division any civil appeal made to the Court of Appeal.

sections.label: Appeal leave point of law
sections.summary: Under new section 47(2) of the SCJA Bill, the Court of Appeal may grant leave to appeal an Appellate Division civil decision raising a point of law of public importance.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Next, under the new section 47(2) of the SCJA Bill, the Court of Appeal may grant leave for an appeal against a decision of the Appellate Division in a civil case if the appeal will raise a point of law of public importance.

sections.label: Stare decisis in restructured Supreme Court
sections.summary: The question asks the Senior Minister of State to clarify how existing case precedents will apply in the restructured Supreme Court under stare decisis.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Next, can the Senior Minister of State also clarify how the existing case precedents will apply in the restructured Supreme Court under the principle of stare decisis?

sections.label: New Appellate Division of High Court
sections.summary: A new Appellate Division of the High Court will hear most appeals from judgments in civil cases originally heard by the High Court.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: First, there will be a new Appellate Division of the High Court, which will hear most appeals from judgments in civil cases originally heard by the High Court.

sections.label: Call to review Judges' retirement age
sections.summary: The speaker repeats the call for the Government to review the retirement age of Supreme Court Judges, to retire later, say at 70.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: To serve these purposes, we would like to repeat our call for the Government to review the retirement age of Supreme Court Judges, to retire later, say, at 70 instead.

sections.label: Extending Judges' retirement age to 70
sections.summary: The speaker says judging is brain work, not physically demanding, so extending Judges' retirement age to 70 is feasible, letting them work longer with security of tenure.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Being a Judge requires brain work but is not physically demanding.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: We believe extending the retirement age of Judges to 70 is entirely feasible, to let our Judges work longer with security of tenure, which will be superior to having short-term Judges.

sections.label: Supreme Court Judge retirement age 65
sections.summary: Supreme Court Judges must be protected from political pressures, but unlike other appointments save the Attorney-General, they have a mandatory retirement age of 65, or at most six months after.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In essence, they must be protected from political pressures from the hon Members of this House so that the quality and integrity of their judgments is unimpeachable.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: However, unlike all other appointments in Singapore, save the Attorney-General, a Supreme Court Judge has a mandatory retirement age of 65, or at most six months after then, specified in the Constitution itself.

sections.label: Constitution Amendment Bill retirement age
sections.summary: The Constitution (Amendment) Bill deletes and substitutes the retirement age provision in essentially the same terms.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Today's Constitution (Amendment) Bill deletes and substitutes the retirement age provision in essentially the same terms.

sections.label: Supreme Court Judges retirement age
sections.summary: The retirement age of 65 for Supreme Court Judges was long older than the norm and is still higher than the general retirement age of 62.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: For many decades the retirement age of 65 for Supreme Court Judges was considerably older than the norm in Singapore and is still higher than the general retirement age of 62 today.

sections.label: UK judges retirement debate and appeals
sections.summary: The UK debates raising the mandatory retirement age for Supreme Court judges above 70, and section 29C(2) provides for appeals from the General Division to the Court of Appeal.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In the UK today, there is an ongoing debate about whether to raise the mandatory retirement age for Supreme Court judges above 70.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: That debate is an urgent one, created by the difficulty of finding suitable candidates for office who are both distinguished in the law and yet not too long in years.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: We do not want to leave it too late to have that discussion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Section 29C(2) provides for an appeal from the General Division of the High Court to the Court of Appeal if the Sixth Schedule or any other written law so provides.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Section 1 of the Sixth Schedule provides that for the purposes of section 29C(2), an appeal against the decision of the General Division in the exercise of its original or appellate civil jurisdiction is to be made to the Court of Appeal in the list of cases provided under A to J.

sections.label: Court of Appeal transfer of appeals
sections.summary: Under section 29D, the Court of Appeal may transfer two specific types of appeal to itself.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Next, on section 29D, the Bill provides that under section 29D, the Court of Appeal may transfer two specific types of appeal to itself: (a) an appeal against any decision of the General Division that has been made to the Appellate Division and (b) when an order under section 39A of the Land Acquisition Act is in force, any appeal made to the Appellate Division under section 29(2) or 38(2) of the Land Acquisition Act.

sections.label: Judicial Commissioners and High Court Judges tenure
sections.summary: Judicial Commissioners and older High Court Judges are contractually renewed without tenure under Articles 95 clauses (2) and (5).

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Currently, our Judicial Commissioners and older High Court Judges are contractually renewed and do not have tenure under Articles 95 clauses (2) and (5) of the Constitution, meaning that they do not have the certainty of staying on in the judiciary.

sections.label: Extending Judges retirement age to 70
sections.summary: The speaker urges extending the retirement age of Judges to 70 with optional retirement at 65, noting US, England and Australia comparisons.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In addition to security of tenure for Judicial Commissioners and Senior Judges to safeguard their judicial independence, I urge the Minister to consider extending the retirement age of Judges to 70, with optional retirement at 65, instead of having renewal of appointments, so that we can still retain the services of older yet experienced and able Judges.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: As a comparison to other jurisdictions, the tenure for judges in the US is for life, while the retirement age of judges in England and Australia is 70.

sections.label: CareShield Life premium equality debate
sections.summary: The Member says he and other Members raised in the CareShield Life Bill debate that differentiated premiums for men and women go against the right to equality.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: With other Members of this House, I had raised in the debate on the CareShield Life Bill that the differentiated premiums for men and women goes against the right to equality.

sections.label: Legislative policies and constitutional equality
sections.summary: The Member states that legislative policies must also be aligned to the right to equality in the Constitution.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: The main point here is that I would like to say that legislative policies must also be aligned to the right to equality in our Constitution.

sections.label: Judicial tenure and defending constitutionality
sections.summary: The Member says Judges' security of tenure enables judicial independence and checks on the Executive and Legislature, and that Parliamentarians must defend the constitutionality of laws they make.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: The security of tenure for our Judges enables full judicial independence and, therefore, further upholds our Constitution ideal by providing effective check and balance on the powers of the Executive and the Legislature.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: Someone once said, "The strength of the Constitution lies in the determination of each citizen to defend it." Therefore, together with our colleagues in the Judiciary, our duty as Parliamentarians must be to defend the constitutionality of the laws that we make in this House for Singaporeans.

sections.label: Choosing Appellate Division Judges
sections.summary: The Member queries how and how many Appellate Division Judges are to be chosen, concerned that drawing only from existing High Court Judges could cause a cannibalisation effect.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: My query is in relation to how and how many Appellate Division Judges are to be chosen.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: If we were to draw just from the existing cohort of High Court Judges, I am concerned that there could be a "cannibalisation" effect.

sections.label: No distinction General Division and SICC
sections.summary: Citing increasing complexity of cases and voluminous documents in local civil cases, the Member suggests as policy there should be no distinction between the General Division and SICC.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: With the increasing complexity of cases and voluminous documents involved in local civil cases, I would respectfully suggest that, as a matter of policy, there should be no distinction drawn between the General Division and SICC.

sections.label: Direct appeal and SCJA amendment
sections.summary: The Member notes subparagraph (j) provides direct appeal to the Court of Appeal under specific legislation, and welcomes clarification that an amendment will change the operative word to time not date.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: I note from subparagraph (j), it is stated that there would be a direct appeal to the Court of Appeal if it is so provided under a specific piece of legislation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: I note with pleasure that the hon Senior Minister of State has clarified that he will be moving an amendment in the Committee stage of this Bill in respect of the proposed section 29B(2) of SCJA which would clarify that the operative word there should be "time" and not "date".

sections.label: Leave despite public importance point
sections.summary: The speaker notes proposed section 47(4)(a) of SCJA allows leave to be refused even if the appeal raises a point of law of public importance, and supports the amendment Bills.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: I note that the test is whether or not an appeal would raise an issue or point of law of public importance.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: However, my concern lies with the proposed section 47(4)(a) of SCJA because it is stated there that leave may not be granted even if the appeal would raise a point of law of public importance.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Notwithstanding my comments, I support the amendment Bills to the SCJA, JRA and the Constitution.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
sentences.text: I did not speak on fixed-term Judges in Singapore and independence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: I apologise to him for remembering the speech wrongly.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: I think it was Ms Anthea Ong who made the point.

sections.label: Appellate Division Judges and precedence
sections.summary: At least three High Court Judges are expected to be appointed to the Appellate Division, and the order of precedence runs from Court of Appeal to Appellate Division to General Division.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Mr Dennis Tan and Mr Murali Pillai asked about the expected increase in the number of Judges.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: We expect at least three Judges from the current High Court to be appointed to the Appellate Division, and additional appointments to the General Division may be made as may be necessary once the Appellate Division has been set up.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: He also asked how persuasive a decision of the Appellate Division will be compared to that of the Court of Appeal.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: It is quite clear, and the order of precedence as set out in the Bill, is as follows, from the highest to the lowest: first, decisions of the Court of Appeal, which remains the apex Court of the land; next, the Appellate Division of the High Court; and then the decisions of the General Division of the High Court.

sections.label: Transfer to Court of Appeal
sections.summary: A case ordinarily allocated to the Appellate Division may be transferred to the Court of Appeal if it requires a decision the apex Court can usefully provide.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Even if a case is ordinarily allocated to the Appellate Division, there is flexibility for it to be transferred to the Court of Appeal, if it requires a decision that the apex Court of the land can usefully provide.

sections.label: Land Acquisition Act appeal transfers
sections.summary: The transfer power in clause 12, introducing sections 29B and 29E of SCJA, refers to the Land Acquisition Act so appeals under sections 29(2) and 38(2) can be transferred like civil appeals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The transfer power in clause 12 which will introduce sections 29B and 29E of SCJA refers to the Land Acquisition Act so that appeals under sections 29(2) and 38(2) of the Land Acquisition Act can be transferred in a manner similar to all the civil appeals.

sections.label: Public importance point for leave
sections.summary: Under the proposed amendments, an appeal must raise a point of law of public importance for leave to be considered.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Under our proposed amendments, it is a requirement that the appeal ought to raise a point of law of public importance for leave to be considered.

sections.label: Professional disciplinary cases jurisdiction
sections.summary: Asked whether the Appellate Division can hear professional disciplinary cases, the speaker says judicial precedent clarifies the Court of Appeal has no civil appellate jurisdiction in lawyer disciplinary proceedings.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Mr Murali Pillai asked whether the Appellate Division has jurisdiction to hear professional disciplinary cases.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: I think judicial precedent has clarified that the Court of Appeal has no civil appellate jurisdiction in disciplinary proceedings for lawyers.

sections.label: Drafting change to Sixth Schedule
sections.summary: The change neatens up drafting provisions and does not alter the minimum number of Judges required under the existing Sixth Schedule.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The change in the arrangement is one of drafting – trying to neaten up the provisions – and does not effect any change to the minimum number of Judges required to hear the categories of cases set out in the existing Sixth Schedule.

sections.label: Single Judge High Court hearings
sections.summary: The Bill retains single Judge hearings in the High Court except as provided in written law, with the SICC as the exception.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: This Bill retains the existing position where a single Judge shall hear proceedings in the High Court, except as provided for in written law.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: And that one exception is the SICC, where proceedings might be heard by a single Judge or three Judges.

sections.label: Amendment to section 29B(2)
sections.summary: The amendment to section 29B(2) will be taken up.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: On section 29B(2), again, we will be taking up the amendment.

sections.label: World Bank rule of law ranking
sections.summary: The World Bank's Worldwide Governance Indicators rank Singapore in the 97th percentile worldwide for rule of law.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: I think I have answered this earlier when I outlined some statistics, but I would say quite clearly so.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: I mentioned the World Bank's Worldwide Governance Indicators ranking Singapore in the 97th percentile worldwide in terms of rule of law.

sections.label: Trust in legal system survey
sections.summary: A Ministry survey showed that 92% of Singaporeans have trust and confidence in the legal system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: In a survey conducted by my Ministry – I cited this earlier – showed that 92% of Singaporeans have trust and confidence in our legal system.

sections.label: Judicial remuneration and protection
sections.summary: The Government keeps judicial remuneration competitive to attract and retain quality persons and protects the Judiciary from baseless attacks, as reflected in the 2016 Act.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: To this end, the Government ensures that remuneration for judicial appointment holders remains competitive so that we are able to attract and retain persons of high quality, ability, integrity and, certainly, of an incorruptible character.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: We are also firm about protecting our Judiciary from baseless attacks against their reputation, as reflected by the adoption of the Administration of Justice (Protection) Act in 2016.

sections.label: State Courts tenure and survey
sections.summary: State Courts handle 95% of judicial matters without security of tenure, yet surveys show respondents agree courts act independently and fairly.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Members who practise in the State Courts will know they deal with and dispose of 95% of all judicial matters in Singapore, but have no security of tenure.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Yet, the 2018 Court Users Survey shows that 99% of respondents agree that the Courts independently carry out justice according to the law.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: And 100% of respondents agree that the Courts administer justice fairly to all in Singapore, regardless of race, language or religion.

sections.label: Supreme Court Bench renewal balance
sections.summary: The system balances renewal of the Supreme Court Bench with tapping Judicial Commissioners and retaining Senior Judges' experience.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: This is also a point I think very graphically recognised by Assoc Prof Walter Theseira when he talked about ossification.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: So, the system we have put in place strikes that balance – works for us, strikes that balance, allows for the appropriate renewal of the Supreme Court Bench in a fair and systematic manner, but also gives us the ability to tap on Judicial Commissioners and also to retain the wide-ranging experience of the Senior Judges.

sections.label: Small country limited talent pool
sections.summary: Singapore is a small country with a limited talent pool.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: What is clear is that we are a small country, with a limited talent pool.

sections.label: Court process enhancements and amendment
sections.summary: Proposed enhancements aim to sustain high standards and access to justice, and an amendment replaces 'date' with 'time' in section 29B(2).

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Together with the other proposed enhancements to the Court processes, it is designed to sustain, in the long term, the high standards of excellence and access to justice that Singapore’s Courts are known for in and outside Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Yes, Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That in page 7, line 26, to leave out the word 'date' and insert the word 'time'".

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: This applies in the context of section 29B(2) of the underlying legislation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: I had addressed this point earlier in my speech.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: I believe this clarifies the position and makes it clear that it is the time that is applicable and not the date from which the Order is made, that the requirement for leave for further arguments to be filed runs.
